problem: Existing automatic photo composition either crops a fixed image, or in drone cinematography relies on heuristics (rule of thirds, shot templates) and tracked subjects. No prior work explores an unknown environment through movement to capture a photo that is optimal under a learned aesthetics model.
motivation: Learned aesthetics models capture human preferences better than explicit heuristics, but view optimization against them cannot be formulated analytically, and cropping-trained aesthetics models are not robust across viewpoints, exposure, or small translations. The paper therefore uses RL to learn a navigation controller against a learned aesthetic reward, together with an aesthetics model built for cross-view comparison.
key_idea: Train an actor-critic (PPO, LSTM) agent in simulation with a shaped reward from a robust learned aesthetics model and an adaptive local-region score threshold, so it navigates to a well-composed view and then triggers a CAPTURE action.
insight: The ablations show that the shaped step reward (score difference plus exploration), LSTM memory, and multilayer aesthetic features all matter. Removing the LSTM drops Gibson from 81.7 to 62.7, and removing multilayer features drops it to 62.3. The learned policy beats greedy and key-frame baselines at the same ~16-step budget, so its advantage comes from efficient exploration rather than from more steps. Adding robustness losses lets the aesthetics model rank across viewpoints (AVA 84.4 vs 62.2) at a small cost on CPC.
method: Problem formulation: a POMDP where the state is the current view plus LSTM memory; the actions are forward/back 0.25 m, turns of 10/30/90° left or right, and CAPTURE, which terminates the episode.
Reward: the CAPTURE reward is +1 if the aesthetic score exceeds the threshold and -1 otherwise. Step reward = φ(s_{t+1})-φ(s_t) + 0.1·0.9999^ζ exploration bonus - 0.005·t time penalty.

Aesthetics model: ResNet18 with a blur-pool antialiasing layer, trained on CPC and AVA with a pairwise ranking loss (same genre for AVA). It adds an MSE similarity loss against minimally cropped images and an exposure ranking loss against brightness-perturbed images (λ=0.6).

Adaptive threshold: τ = μ+σ of the scores of the K=100 nearest views among 2000 sampled per scene near the start pose, roughly the top 16% of local views. Start poses with very low scores are re-sampled during training only.

Policy architecture: the aesthetics model's four residual-block outputs are average-pooled and concatenated, then passed to an MLP and LSTM backbone with actor and critic heads. Training uses PPO (stable-baselines) for 1.5M steps on 61 Gibson scenes.
Sim-to-real deployment: run on a Clearpath Jackal with a webcam at 1.5 m via ROS, re-querying the policy if an action would cause a collision.

setting.backbone: ResNet18 aesthetics model + MLP+LSTM actor-critic (PPO), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Aesthetics: CPC + AVA (210k iterations). RL: 1.5M steps on 61 Gibson scenes in Habitat. Imitation baseline used 17K demonstrations.
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: forward/back 0.25 m, turn 10°/30°/90° left/right, CAPTURE
setting.simulator: Habitat (Gibson train; Gibson and Replica eval)
setting.privileged: The aesthetic threshold in simulation is computed from densely sampled views (2000 per scene) of the scene, used for the reward and evaluation. In the real world the threshold is not available (evaluated via a human study).

numbers.extra: median 16 steps; baselines capped at 16 steps
numbers.evidence: Table II: Accuracy in Achieving the Aesthetic Threshold, Gibson 81.7 ± 0.9

numbers.eval_set_note: 18 Replica scenes, zero-shot transfer from Gibson training
64 real photos, 1792 judgements from 28 valid AMT surveys
numbers.extra: real Clearpath Jackal; preference vs initial view
numbers.evidence: the mean preference score is 0.63 ± 0.01 (standard error)

numbers_note: Metric is % of captured photos exceeding the aesthetic threshold (Acc_thresh). No standard navigation benchmark metrics such as SR/SPL are reported.
results: AutoPhoto reaches 81.7% (Gibson) and 77.8% (Replica) of photos above the aesthetic threshold, versus 57.8% (Imitation Learning) and 56.8% (Key Frame Selection) on Gibson and 56.6% (Key Frame Selection) on Replica. In the real-world AMT study, humans preferred its photos over the initial view with a mean score of 0.63.
limitations: Depends on high-quality simulated environments and on the choice of aesthetic function, which strongly influences behavior.
Real-world evaluation only compares against the initial view; the action space is limited to a ground robot with planar motion.
